note: A declarative sentence ends in a question mark after the split.
replacement: In the same way, if the uncooling or warm principle were imperishable, then when cold attacked the fire, the fire would not have perished or been put out, but would have gone away unaffected?

note: Address "my friend" before Simmias is dropped.
replacement: I am convinced, Socrates, said Cebes, and I have no further objection. But if my friend Simmias, or anyone else, has something more to say, he had better speak out and not stay silent. I do not know what other occasion he can put it off to, if he wants to say something or hear something said.

The wise and orderly soul follows the straight path and is aware of its surroundings. But the soul that desires the body, as I said before, has long fluttered around the lifeless body and the visible world. After many struggles and much suffering, it is carried off with difficulty and by force by its attendant genius. When it arrives at the place where the other souls are gathered, if it is impure and has done impure deeds, such as foul murders or other crimes akin to these, the works of brothers in crime, then everyone flees from that soul and turns away. No one will be its companion or its guide, and it wanders alone in utter misery until certain times are fulfilled. When they are fulfilled, it is carried irresistibly to the dwelling that fits it. In the same way every pure and just soul, which has passed through life in the company and under the guidance of the gods, has its own proper home.

note: "Although..." is left as a sentence fragment.
replacement: If I had the art of Glaucus, Simmias, replied Socrates, I would tell you, although I do not know that even the art of Glaucus could prove my tale true, and I could never prove it myself; and even if I could, Simmias, I fear my life would end before the argument was finished. I can, however, describe the shape of the earth and its regions as I conceive them.
